name: stb-image-opt
baseline: upstream stb_image.h v2.30 (nothings/stb at 2c980bb), compiled the way consumers compile it (-O2)
workload: Image decode time in ns per pixel (minimum of 7 repeats, 0.1 s budget per repeat, pinned with taskset) over a 14-file mixed suite (7 PNG, 4 JPEG, 1 GIF, 1 PSD, 1 HDR; mostly small synthetic 512x512 and 640x480 images plus PNGSuite files) with req_comp=0, plus a req_comp=4 JPEG run.
claimed_speedup: About +10% geomean over upstream -O2 on the mixed suite; PNG decode +8.6% geomean (isolated A/B); palette PNG +29%; GIF +21%; progressive JPEG +19%; JPEG to RGBA (req_comp=4) about +13% geomean; AVX2 YCbCr kernel 1.63x and AVX2 IDCT pair kernel 1.70x versus the SSE2 kernels in the same header (isolated microbenchmarks). The README also states the AVX2 IDCT adds about +8% (req_comp=0) and about +14% (req_comp=4) on JPEG decoding.
compiler_and_flags: clang 23.1.2. Baseline: upstream header at -O2. Fork: -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 -ffp-contract=off plus multi-workload PGO trained on a held-out corpus (harness/bench_vs_upstream.sh). AVX2 kernels are runtime-dispatched via CPUID and XGETBV.
hardware: Intel Core i7-14700F (Raptor Lake), WSL2, benchmark process pinned to one core with taskset
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; first commit 2026-09-28; releases up to v1.3.0
tradeoffs: Only src/stb_image.h changes (+539/-10 lines, additive and guarded), so it stays a single drop-in header with unchanged API and ABI. AVX2 JPEG kernels (YCbCr to RGB, two-block IDCT) are selected at runtime and fall back to SSE2 or scalar on other CPUs; non-x86 targets cross-compile but get no SIMD gain. Output is bit-identical to upstream: README and NOTES.md report 12,306 differential checks (stbi_load req_comp 0-4, stbi_load_16, stbi_loadf, GIF frames, stbi_info) on every dispatch path with clang, gcc and zig cc, plus ASan/UBSan and libFuzzer runs. Prebuilt static libraries for Linux (glibc, musl, ARM64) and Windows are attached to releases. Scope is decode only.
caveats: The baseline is upstream stb_image, not libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp or libavif, so this says nothing about the listed incumbents. The headline compares the fork built with -O3 and held-out PGO against upstream built with -O2 and no PGO, so compiler flags are mixed into the source-change gain; NOTES.md says flags alone move little and held-out PGO is worth about +6.3%. Source-only A/B figures (same flags, pre-change build): PNG +8.6% geomean, IDCT +7.7% (req_comp=0) and +13.7% (req_comp=4). Results/summary.csv (opened at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aplghl/stb-image-opt/HEAD/results/summary.csv) shows GEOMEAN 1.1010 over 14 files with two rows slightly below 1.0 (hdr_range.hdr 0.986, plasma_512.psd 0.995). The suite is PNG-heavy and uses small synthetic images; the README says numbers are single-machine and load-sensitive, and NOTES.md says per-file ratios under about 3% are noise. Unofficial fork, not endorsed by the upstream author, single author, repository created 2026-09-28 with no outside users yet. The per-kernel speedups are against the fork's own SSE2 path, not against upstream.

name: stb-image-write-opt
baseline: upstream stb_image_write.h v1.16 (nothings/stb at 2c980bb), compiled the way consumers compile it (-O2)
workload: Image encode time in ns per pixel (minimum of several repeats, pinned with taskset) over 17 rows: PNG (1-4 components, several quality/filter settings, palette and random inputs), JPEG (quality 50/75/90), BMP, TGA and HDR output, from deterministic synthetic 512x512 plasma, 640x480 gradient and generated pixel inputs.
claimed_speedup: +62.7% geomean on the mixed suite with held-out PGO (about +50% without PGO); PNG encode 1.62-2.15x; JPEG encode 1.63-2.04x; isolated deflate match kernel (stbiw__zlib_countm, SSE2 vs scalar) about 3.3x and whole deflate 3.4x (0.43 vs 1.47 ns/byte); downstream consumer program PNG 1.90x and JPEG 1.17x.
compiler_and_flags: clang 23.1.2. Baseline: upstream header at -O2. Fork: -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 -ffp-contract=off plus held-out PGO. The exact build is also verified at -march=x86-64-v3, scalar (-DSTBIW_NO_SIMD), gcc 13.3 and zig cc.
hardware: Intel Core i7-14700F (Raptor Lake), 28 threads, WSL2, Ubuntu 24.04, benchmark pinned with taskset
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; 2 commits, both 2026-09-29; release v1.0.0
tradeoffs: Only src/stb_image_write.h changes; public API and ABI unchanged (16 exported symbols checked by make abi). Output is byte-identical to upstream across about 9,600 differential checks (5 formats x 1-4 components x quality/filter/stride/RLE/flip toggles), with a make nonvacuous test that deliberately corrupted output must fail the suite. Changes: SSE2 DEFLATE match-length kernel (baseline x86-64, no runtime dispatch, scalar fallback on other targets), precomputed bit-reversed fixed-Huffman codes, and binary search over length/distance code tables. Recommended flags -march=x86-64-v2 need SSE4.2-class CPUs. Encode side only.
caveats: The baseline is upstream stb_image_write, not libpng, zlib, libjpeg-turbo or libwebp; stb's PNG encoder is a low-effort zlib implementation, so these ratios do not rank it against the listed incumbents. The headline mixes source changes with compiler flags: the README's list of source changes covers only the DEFLATE/PNG path, and it says the recommended build also enables compiler auto-vectorization of the JPEG encoder, so the JPEG gain appears to come from -O3, -march=x86-64-v2 and PGO against an upstream -O2 build rather than from JPEG source changes. The 17-row geomean includes BMP, TGA and HDR rows that docs/MEASUREMENT.md and results/README.md call plumbing-bound and layout-sensitive (hdr 0.948, tga 1.07, bmp 1.56 in results/summary.csv, opened at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aplghl/stb-image-write-opt/HEAD/results/summary.csv, GEOMEAN 1.627); the README says not to read a speedup from them. The downstream consumer benchmark (public API, prebuilt library, results/consumer.csv) gives a smaller PNG 1.90x and JPEG 1.17x, geomean 1.49x. The about +50% no-PGO figure appears only in the README text, not in a results file I opened. Synthetic inputs, single machine under WSL2, run-to-run variation of a few percent. Unofficial fork not endorsed by the upstream author, single author, two commits.

name: intel-tex-rs-2 (intel_tex_2)
baseline: intel-tex-rs-2 main before PR #50, i.e. the vendored Intel ISPCTextureCompressor kernels built with ISPC 1.20 (the PR does not compare against a separately built Intel ispc_texcomp binary)
workload: Single-threaded texture block encode time per format and preset on a 256x256 image (criterion benchmark: bc1, bc3, bc4, bc5, bc6h and bc7 presets, bc7 opaque and alpha, etc1), plus a full 4096x4096 texture (examples/lambertian.jpg) across all presets.
claimed_speedup: PR #50 (merged 2026-09-28) title: BC6H 1.8-3.1x, BC7 2.1-6.2x and ETC1 6.1x faster; BC1-BC5 unchanged. Per-row examples (256x256, 1 thread): bc7_opaque/basic 51.07 ms to 20.14 ms (2.54x) and bc7_alpha/basic 68.44 ms to 13.18 ms (5.19x) versus main on ISPC 1.20; versus PR #49 (the same kernels rebuilt with ISPC 1.31) bc7_opaque/basic 49.37 ms to 20.14 ms (2.45x) and bc7_alpha/basic 68.21 ms to 13.18 ms (5.18x); bc6h/fast 3.10x, bc7_alpha/slow 6.18x, etc1 6.06x; 2.35x total across all presets at 4096x4096.
compiler_and_flags: ISPC 1.31 (LLVM 23) after PR #49, Apple CPU targets pinned (apple-a14 for macOS builds); Rust release profile lto = true, opt-level = 3, codegen-units = 1 (Cargo.toml); harness is criterion (cargo bench -- --save-baseline main, then --baseline main) as described in the PR text.
hardware: Apple M5 Max (ARM64 NEON), 1 thread; x86, Windows, Linux and Android binaries were regenerated but not benchmarked
stars_or_usage: 17 stars, 3 forks; published on crates.io as intel_tex_2 0.5.0
tradeoffs: Rust bindings over prebuilt ISPC kernels (ISPC and libclang only needed with --features ispc to regenerate; binaries for macOS, iOS, Android, Linux and Windows are committed in the repo). Speedups came from removing per-lane gathers (NEON has no gather), inlining helpers, hoisting subset work and sharing work between modes, which also made fully inlined kernels much slower to compile (generate-binaries CI jobs went from about 2/3/4 minutes to 17/23/45 minutes on macOS/Linux/Windows). Quality: PSNR change within 0.0001 dB for BC1, BC3 and BC7, worst single image -0.006 dB (BC6H); ETC1 final commits changed tie-breaking so about 10% of blocks differ with equal or better PSNR. Kernels derive from the discontinued Intel ISPCTextureCompressor, now vendored from Traverse Research's fork. ASTC is listed as pending in the README.
caveats: The lead's framing (2.1-6.2x faster than Intel ispc_texcomp) is not what the PR measures: the baseline is the crate's own previous main, which is the Intel kernels built with ISPC 1.20, so the gain is against an older build of the same lineage. Only Apple Silicon was measured, and much of the gain comes from avoiding gathers that are expensive on NEON, so the x86 gain is unknown (PR #51 says the same about its own estimator changes). I could not find the criterion benchmark code in the repository tree (no benches/ directory on main; PR #50 has two commits, 'Update vendor to the fork's ARM64 performance work' and 'Regenerate binaries with the optimized kernels'), so the numbers are not reproducible from the repo as read; hence tier C, not A. PR text was read through a page summarizer on two separate fetches that agreed on the headline figures and sample rows; treat per-row values as quoted, not verbatim copies. The repo commits page for main still showed 2026-07-01 as latest while the PR list shows PRs #49, #50 and #51 merged 2026-09-28 (last_commit uses the merge date). Related same-day evidence at https://github.com/Traverse-Research/intel-tex-rs-2/pull/51 (BC7 bc7e-style partition ranking, opaque presets 1.04-1.73x faster than the post-#50 state on 24 Kodak images, Apple M5 Max, 1 thread; on a 4K texture the PR says bc7e is slower than the new kernel at every comparable quality level, e.g. veryfast 2.38 s vs 1.05 s at 51.27 dB and basic 8.84 s vs 5.21 s); this could be a stronger third-party-baseline entry once the harness is public.

name: bc7enc_rdo
baseline: Intel ispc_texcomp (BC7 slow, basic, fast and ultrafast profiles); also Microsoft DirectXTex CPU BC7 encoder
workload: Total BC7 encode time and average PSNR (perceptual REC709 luma PSNR, and plain RGB PSNR) over 31 images (kodim corpus plus others), multithreaded with OpenMP, encode time only, bc7enc16-lineage encoder (modes 1 and 6 only, not vectorized) versus ispc_texcomp profiles (called 64 blocks at a time, AVX) and DirectXTex.
claimed_speedup: Perceptual metric: ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s at 48.6 dB versus bc7enc16 uber0/max_partitions 64 38.3 s at 49.6 dB (9.3x faster and 1.0 dB higher, derived from page data); ispc_texcomp basic 100.2 s at 48.3 dB versus 20.8 s at 49.3 dB (4.8x, derived); ispc_texcomp fast 41.5 s at 48.0 dB versus 20.8 s at 49.3 dB (2.0x, derived); ispc_texcomp ultrafast 1.9 s at 46.2 dB versus 8.9 s at 48.4 dB (bc7enc16 about 4.7x slower, derived). Non-perceptual RGB PSNR: ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s at 46.8 dB versus 29.3 s at 45.8 dB (12.1x faster, derived, but 1.0 dB lower) and versus 51 s at 46.1 dB (7.0x, derived); ispc_texcomp fast 41.45 s at 46.09 dB versus the latest bc7enc16 41.42 s at 46.03 dB (parity, README says 'just as fast as ispc_texcomp fast'); ispc_texcomp ultrafast 1.9 s at 42.7 dB versus 3.8 s at 42.7 dB (bc7enc16 2x slower). DirectXTex CPU default (no 3-subset modes) 9485.1 s at 45.6 dB versus bc7enc16 uber1/max_partitions 64 36 s at 46.0 dB (about 263x, derived); DirectXTex mode-6-only 466.4 s at 41.9 dB versus 6.7 s at 42.8 dB (about 70x, derived).
hardware: Dual Xeon workstation (CPU model not stated), OpenMP multithreaded (thread count not stated); ispc_texcomp used AVX instructions
stars_or_usage: 282 stars, 62 forks; encoder lineage also in bc7enc and bc7enc16
tradeoffs: Per the LICENSE file the repo's own code is MIT or Unlicense (public domain, no patent grant), the bundled bc7e.ispc is Apache-2.0 and LodePNG is zlib-style. No third-party dependencies for the encoder (C++11, drop-in files rgbcx.cpp, bc7enc.cpp, ert.cpp). Builds with cmake; SUPPORT_BC7E=TRUE adds bc7e.ispc and needs Intel's ISPC compiler. bc7enc.cpp is the 4-mode non-ISPC encoder with optional reduced-entropy mode; bc7e.ispc supports all modes but not reduced entropy. RDO post-processing (ert.cpp) works with any block format, tuned for Deflate, LZHAM or LZMA, and the README claims 10-50% size reductions after LZ compression. The README now points to bc7f as an even faster analytical alternative.
caveats: These tables are no longer in the current README (checked: the 2026 README has no benchmark tables); they are in the 2021-02-13 README at commit 0db1ba2, inherited from bc7enc16, so they describe the predecessor encoder (modes 1 and 6, no SIMD), not the current bc7enc_rdo or its bundled bc7e.ispc. The README says most timings are for the original release, and later versions are about 8-27% faster at the same quality. The README names only 'a dual Xeon workstation' and OpenMP; no CPU model, compiler, flags or thread count is given, so tier C (and the DirectXTex ratios of about 70x and 263x are implausibly large for an unstated setup, and the README notes it used a locally patched DirectXTex build, so cap at C). The perceptual win is measured with the encoder's own optimization target (weighted YCbCr luma PSNR), and the non-perceptual RGB result trades 1.0 dB for speed. The ultrafast profile is faster in ispc_texcomp. The old README also claims the BC1 encoder is 3-4x faster than libsquish cluster fit with SSE2 and faster than AMD Compressonator, with no numbers. Commits since at least 2021-09-13 in the visible history are all README edits (latest 2026-07-31, bc7f note), so the code itself looks unchanged for years (status stale). The lead's check of README tables against bc7e and Compressonator found nothing in the current README; a WebSearch snippet suggests a Compressonator-versus-bc7e comparison exists elsewhere but I did not open it. claimed_speedup: Values read off the relative-performance chart image (approximate, the changelog text gives no numbers): astcenc-avx2 2.0 versus astcenc 1.7 at about the same PSNR (delta about 0 to -0.2 dB for nearly all points): -thorough about 2.1-3.1x, -medium about 1.7-3.8x (most points 2.2-3.5x), -fast about 1.3-4.0x (most points 1.9-3.4x). Later series on the same CPU: 4.0 -thorough versus 3.7 about 1.2-1.75x at near-equal PSNR (chart). Text claims in the current README and 5.x changelog: each step from SSE2 to SSE4.1 to AVX2 gains about 15%, and the reference C build (ASTCENC_ISA_NONE) is about 3.25 times slower than the SSE2 build.
compiler_and_flags: astcenc-avx2 binary (AVX2, SSE4.2, POPCNT, F16C); compiler and optimization flags are not stated on the changelog pages. Repo CMake uses -flto=auto for GCC and -ffp-model=precise with -ffp-contract=on for Clang in non-invariant builds.

stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars, 286 forks; official Arm ASTC reference-quality encoder; latest series 5.7.0 (August 2026)
tradeoffs: Quality presets (-fastest to -exhaustive) trade compression time against PSNR. Multiple prebuilt ISA variants (SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2, NEON, SVE 128 and 256, RISC-V vector backend). Codec library API is not binary compatible across versions. Builds are bit-exact across platforms by default; the NO_INVARIANCE option gives up to 5-20% more speed for up to 0.2 dB lower quality (4.0 changelog). 2.0 changed the command line and added a library API.

name: mozjpeg
workload: None. The project documents compression speed as a deliberate cost of smaller files (trellis quantization, optimized Huffman tables, progressive scans with jpegrescan).
claimed_speedup: No speed advantage claimed. README-mozilla.txt states that with default settings mozjpeg is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo or even libjpeg at compressing, that its performance is highly asymmetric (compression much slower than decompression) and that it is not suitable for real-time compression.
stars_or_usage: 5.7k stars, 435 forks; widely deployed in web image pipelines
tradeoffs: Speed and size trade-off versus libjpeg-turbo: slower compression by design in exchange for smaller files; decompression speed is the inherited libjpeg-turbo SIMD speed. Every mozjpeg improvement can be switched off at run time, in which case it behaves like libjpeg-turbo. Drop-in libjpeg API and ABI, strict superset of libjpeg-turbo features. Maintainers ask that non-mozjpeg-specific fixes go to libjpeg-turbo. Third-party estimates found (not measurements from this repo): libvips maintainer in https://github.com/libvips/libvips/discussions/2045 says libjpeg-turbo is perhaps 3x to 4x faster on x86 and mozjpeg can give up to perhaps 30% extra compression by adjusting parameters; a user report in https://github.com/mozilla/mozjpeg/issues/13 claims roughly 60% smaller output but almost 10 times longer compression than libjpeg-turbo, without versions, flags or machine.
caveats: No numbers in the project's own documentation, so tier D (notable, 5.7k stars). Versions: GitHub releases page lists v4.1.1 (August 15, 'Updated to libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3'; year not shown on the page), v4.0.3, v4.0.0 (libjpeg-turbo 2); the top entry of master's ChangeLog.md is 3.0.5, the inherited libjpeg-turbo changelog, whose speedup figures (for example 2-3.5x faster decompression than libjpeg) are libjpeg-turbo's, not mozjpeg's own. Last visible commit 2025-06-23 and several 2026 pull requests (for example #453, #455-#457) are open and unmerged, so maintenance is stale. The third-party numbers above were read through page summarizers and have no methodology. The entry is a size-efficiency tool rather than a speed win; it is useful as the baseline of the listed mozjpeg-rs and as a reference for the speed cost of trellis quantization.

name: GPUJPEG
baseline: none in the README; the only comparison found is against NVIDIA nvJPEG in two user issues (not libjpeg-turbo)
workload: README: JPEG encode and decode time per frame for a 16K DCI source image cropped or downscaled to HD (2 Mpix), 4K (8 Mpix), 8K (33 Mpix) and 16K (132 Mpix), RGB input, quality 75, non-interleaved, restart interval 24-36, average of 99 runs excluding the first, gpujpegtool -n 100.
claimed_speedup: No comparative speedup is claimed. README timings only: encode 4K 1.65 ms on RTX 4080, 1.71 ms on RTX 3080, 2.89 ms on RTX 2080 Ti, 3.16 ms on AMD RX 7600 via ZLUDA; encode 8K 6.33 ms (RTX 4080) and 16K 24.92 ms; decode 4K 1.46 ms (RTX 4080) and 8K 5.78 ms; on RTX 3080 8K encode 6.21 ms at quality 70 and 2.28 ms without PCIe transfers. About 4.8 Gpix/s for 4K encode on RTX 4080 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Recommended build cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (optional -DUSE_NATIVE_CPU_ARCH=ON); the README says the RTX 4080 numbers were taken with cmake configured without those flags and that other measurements were made without a Release build type. CUDA toolkit and host compiler versions are not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4080, RTX 3080, RTX 2080 Ti, GTX 1060M, GTX 580 and AMD Radeon RX 7600 via ZLUDA; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA CUDA GPU (AMD only through ZLUDA). Baseline sequential-Huffman JPEG only, 8-bit; GPU Huffman encode and decode require restart markers (with restart interval 0 the CPU Huffman coder is used, because the README says one GPU thread would be very slow), so arbitrary JPEGs from cameras decode without GPU parallelism. Default timings include host-device PCIe transfers (8K encode 6.21 ms versus 2.28 ms without them on RTX 3080). First call has initialization cost (about 28.6 ms for 8K on RTX 3080 in the README). Larger images can run out of memory on small GPUs. COPYING is BSD-2-Clause; the README also says the code contains source provided by NVIDIA Corporation and is based on SiGenGPU.
caveats: No numeric comparison against libjpeg-turbo, nvJPEG or any CPU codec in the README, FAQ.md or NEWS.md, so tier D (reference-quality GPU codec, notable). The only comparison numbers found are two user issues from September 2020 (https://github.com/CESNET/GPUJPEG/issues/47 and https://github.com/CESNET/GPUJPEG/issues/48, read through a summarizer, no maintainer reply visible, GPU model and CUDA version not stated): on a random 8192-labelled image total time was 911.242 ms for GPUJPEG against 1608.21 ms for nvJPEG, but on a portrait with a uniform background it was 620.884 ms against 441.444 ms, so nvJPEG was faster, and the user noted GPUJPEG produced 16384 restart segments against 1 for nvJPEG. These are mixed, old and without methodology. Independent GPU decode papers (for example arXiv 2111.09219, which compares against libjpeg-turbo and nvJPEG) were found in a search snippet but arXiv is blocked here and they do not benchmark GPUJPEG in the snippet. A later check of the README against a CPU baseline is needed before listing it as faster than libjpeg-turbo.
